entries.name: Sumerians
entries.settlement: walled city-states around a temple platform, each with its own god and king
monuments: temple platforms at Uruk and Eridu
entries.beliefs: city gods in temples; humans made to serve the gods; no strong afterlife
entries.fell_by: Akkadian conquest 2334 BCE; final eclipse after Ur III falls to the Elamites 2004 BCE; the language survives only as a priestly tongue until c. 100 BCE
entries.notes: Writing was born keeping grain accounts. The first urban, literate civilization; model cities, not camps.

entries.name: Old Babylonians (Amorite)
entries.settlement: walled capital on the Euphrates with vassal cities of variable loyalty
entries.beliefs: Marduk elevated to head of the pantheon; omens and divination systematized
entries.fell_by: Hittite sack of Babylon c. 1595 BCE and the Kassite takeover
entries.notes: Hammurabi's stele is the era in one object: law graded by class, written on a 2.25 m black diorite pillar.

entries.name: Assyrians
entries.settlement: walled capitals on the Tigris (Assur, Kalhu, Dur-Sharrukin, Nineveh) fed by road and deportation
monuments: palace slabs of Nineveh and Kalhu
trade: tin and textiles along caravan roads
entries.beliefs: Ashur the national god demands empire; the king is his steward; omens govern campaigns
entries.fell_by: Medes and Babylonians sack Nineveh 612 BCE; Harran falls 609 BCE; remnants absorbed into Babylonia and the Aramaic-speaking world
entries.notes: The Neo-Assyrian phase (911-609 BCE) is the first true empire: mass deportation, paved roads, a standing army. Model terror as policy, not madness.

entries.name: Akkadians
entries.settlement: imperial capital at Akkad (unlocated) ruling Sumerian city-states directly
trade: silver and tin from Anatolia and Iran
entries.beliefs: Sargon as divine king; Ishtar of Akkad elevated over the city gods of Sumer
entries.fell_by: Gutian incursions and a long drought; replaced by the Third Dynasty of Ur (Sumerian Renaissance) c. 2112 BCE
entries.notes: The first multi-ethnic empire; Sargon's rise from gardener to king of the world was remembered for 4,000 years.

entries.name: Chaldeans (Neo-Babylonians)
entries.settlement: great walled capital at Babylon; Chaldean tribal migrants ruling older Babylonian cities
trade: spices and luxury goods along the Gulf
entries.beliefs: Marduk supreme; elaborate temple cult; celestial omens as state science
entries.fell_by: Cyrus the Great takes Babylon in 539 BCE, mostly without a battle; Nabonidus exiled to Carmania
entries.notes: The Babylon of the Bible: Nebuchadnezzar exiled the Jews (586 BCE). Astronomy here was calendrical and priestly, not decorative.

entries.name: Amorites
entries.settlement: tribal migrations followed by seizure of city thrones (Babylon, Mari, Larsa, Yamhad)
crafts: cuneiform letters of the Mari archive
trade: caravan trade between Syria and Sumer
entries.beliefs: storm god Amurru cult; western Semitic deities enter Mesopotamia (Hadad, Dagon)
entries.fell_by: absorbed into Babylonian and Assyrian populations by 1500 BCE; Hittites end the Amorite dynasty of Babylon c. 1595 BCE
entries.notes: An Amorite founded Babylon's greatest dynasty. The Mari letters are the best window into a caravan-age court.

entries.name: Kassites
entries.settlement: ruling house over Babylon without a distinct language community; the most durable dynasty in Babylonian history
trade: lapis from Afghanistan via continued Indus and Iranian routes
entries.beliefs: Babylonian pantheon adopted whole; ancestral gods left behind; omens intensify
entries.fell_by: Elamite capture of Babylon 1155 BCE; the dynasty is restored weakly then fades into the Isin II period
entries.notes: They ruled Babylon longer than any dynasty. The Amarna letters are addressed to their kings as great equals of Egypt's pharaohs.

entries.name: Mitanni (Hurrians)
entries.settlement: Hurrian kingdom capital Washukanni (unlocated), elite Indo-Aryan-named aristocracy over a Hurrian majority
monuments: palace cities on the Khabur (Washukanni, unlocated)
crafts: chariot warfare and horse training (the Kikkuli text)
trade: horses and chariots to Egypt and the Hittites
entries.beliefs: Indo-Aryan horse cult over Hurrian gods (Teshub, Shaushka, Kumarbi); diplomatic marriages sealed by treaty oaths
entries.fell_by: Assyrian campaigns under Adad-nirari I and Shalmaneser I; final destruction of Wasukanni c. 1260 BCE; Hittites take the rump under Suppiluliuma I
entries.notes: Their horse-training manual survives in Hittite. A rare state built around chariotry rather than cities.

entries.name: Elamites
entries.settlement: kingdom of Susa and Anshan; recurring rival and intermittent conqueror of Sumer and Babylon
trade: lapis, carnelian and tin eastward and westward
entries.beliefs: Napirisha and Inshushinak; the king as chosen of the gods; ziggurat cult
entries.fell_by: Ashurbanipal sacks Susa 646 BCE; the realm survives weakly; Cyrus takes Susa 539 BCE; the language dies by the 4th century BCE
entries.notes: The perpetual counterweight to Mesopotamian power; they hauled Hammurabi's stele back to Susa as war booty, which is how it survived.

entries.name: Lullubi
entries.settlement: highland chiefdoms, no true cities; known through Akkadian and Assyrian records and rock reliefs
monuments: rock relief of King Anubanini at Darband-i Gaur
crafts: rock relief sculpture (Anubanini's relief at Darband-i Gaur)
trade: timber and stone down to the alluvium
entries.fell_by: absorbed into Assyria, then Urartu and finally Media; disappears as a distinct identity by the first millennium BCE
entries.notes: Famous almost solely for being defeated by Naram-Sin in c. 2254 BCE; the stele is the image everyone draws.

entries.name: Gutians
entries.settlement: foreign dynasty ruling from Sumerian cities without integrating; described as a plague by native writers
entries.fell_by: Utu-hengal of Uruk expelled them c. 2112 BCE; Ur III replaced them
entries.notes: The first great northern invasion, remembered by native writers as a catastrophe; their language is unclassified.

entries.name: Ubaid culture
entries.settlement: large villages and early towns (Eridu, Ur, Tell el-Oueili) organized around a temple sequence
monuments: Eridu temple sequence (rebuilt 17 times in place)
crafts: slow pottery wheel by late phases
trade: carnelian and turquoise down the Gulf
entries.beliefs: temple-centred cult at Eridu; the fish-apkallu motif appears later as a memory of this era
entries.fell_by: absorbed into the Uruk expansion c. 4000-3800 BCE
entries.notes: The first to farm the southern alluvium; houses already tripartite, temple already central. No writing yet.

entries.name: Uruk culture
entries.settlement: first true cities (Uruk, possibly 40-50k people), unwalled at first, run from monumental temple precincts
trade: lapis and carnelian from Afghanistan and India
colony at Habuba Kabira on the Euphrates
entries.beliefs: city god in a monumental temple; Inanna at Uruk; the priest-king as her steward
entries.fell_by: fades into the Jemdet Nasr period and then Early Dynastic Sumer by c. 2900 BCE
entries.notes: The wheel, writing, the city, the temple economy, ration-bowls: all appear here, in one millennium.

entries.name: Hassuna culture
entries.settlement: small farming villages and hamlets of a few hectares, unfortified
dwellings: rectangular tauf (rammed-earth) houses with courtyards and ovens
trade: carnelian and turquoise beads imported from the east
entries.fell_by: superseded by the Halaf and Ubaid expansions c. 5500-5250 BCE
entries.notes: The earliest well-defined farming villages of the north; stamp seals mean property and accounting before cities.

entries.name: Halaf culture
entries.settlement: small hamlets and shrines; circular tholos houses, no cities, no state
dwellings: circular tholoi of mudbrick with domed roofs
crafts: Halaf polychrome pottery (the finest of prehistoric Mesopotamia)
trade: obsidian and exotic stone exchange networks across the north
entries.beliefs: female figurines common; shrines common; no texts survive
entries.fell_by: eclipsed by Ubaid expansion and the Halaf-Ubaid transition c. 5100 BCE
entries.notes: Their pottery is worth modelling on its own: geometric painted swirls on thin walls. No texts, no kings, just villages and clay.

entries.name: Samarra culture
subsistence: early irrigation along the Tigris tributaries
entries.settlement: villages on the central river floodplain (Tell es-Sawwan), larger and more organized than Hassuna
dwellings: rectangular mudbrick houses with buttressed walls and grain bins
trade: exchange up and down the Tigris; obsidian
entries.beliefs: mother-goddess figurines abundant at Tell es-Sawwan; possible shrine architecture
entries.fell_by: absorbed into the Ubaid expansion c. 4800 BCE
entries.notes: The bridge from northern villages to southern irrigation; early signs of canal farming before cities.

entries.name: Arameans
entries.settlement: tribal confederations seizing city thrones (Guzana, etc.); never unified; absorbed politically by Assyria
crafts: alphabetic Aramaic script (ancestral to Hebrew, Syriac, Arabic)
trade: the caravan roads of the Levant and upper Mesopotamia
entries.beliefs: Hadad as storm god; assimilated quickly into local pantheons; later a fertile ground for Christianity
entries.fell_by: political absorption by Assyria and Babylonia; their language conquered the region culturally — Aramaic became the lingua franca
entries.notes: They lost every battle and won the language: Jesus spoke Aramaic. The script on the cliffs is theirs.

entries.name: Babylonian Jews (Galut Bavel)
subsistence: trade, crafts, banking, agriculture in canal villages
entries.settlement: communities in Babylon, Sura, Pumbedita; the academies where the Babylonian Talmud was written
trade: long-distance commerce with the Gulf and Iran
entries.beliefs: rabbinic Judaism; the Babylonian Talmud compiled c. 500 CE
entries.fell_by: community persisted nearly 2,500 years; most emigrated 1950-1951 to Israel after the Farhud pogrom (1941); a few thousand remain today
entries.notes: The Talmud is a Babylonian document. Baghdad's Jewish quarter was one of the largest Jewish communities on Earth before 1941.

entries.name: Achaemenid Persians (Babylon satrapy)
subsistence: tribute and taxation across the empire
entries.settlement: Babylon administered as a satrapy; Persians few, local elites co-opted, Aramaic the chancery language
entries.beliefs: Ahura Mazda; tolerance as policy — Cyrus lets the Jewish exiles return in 538 BCE
entries.fell_by: Alexander takes Babylon 331 BCE; Seleucus inherits the satrapy after 312 BCE
entries.notes: The first multicultural empire; Babylon still the prestige city — Alexander died there in 323 BCE.

entries.name: Seleucids
entries.settlement: Greek cities planted in Babylonia (Seleucia-on-the-Tigris founded c. 305 BCE, eclipsing Babylon itself)
crafts: philosophy (Berossus writes a Babylonian history in Greek)
entries.beliefs: Greek pantheon mapped onto Marduk and Nabu; syncretism official policy
entries.fell_by: Parthians take Seleucia-on-the-Tigris 141 BCE; western rump survives until Pompey and Rome finish it 63 BCE
entries.notes: The Greek layer of Babylon: cuneiform texts were still written in Hellenistic Babylon — the last tablets come from Seleucid-era Uruk.

entries.name: Parthians (Arsacids)
subsistence: camel and horse nomadism on the steppe edge
entries.settlement: loose feudal empire; Ctesiphon founded across the Tigris from Seleucia as winter capital
entries.beliefs: Zoroastrian and syncretic cults; local gods tolerated; Greek remains in the cities
entries.fell_by: Ardashir I defeats Artabanus IV at Hormozdgān 224 CE; Sasanian Persia begins
entries.notes: Rome's great rival across the Euphrates for four centuries; the iwan (vaulted hall open on one side) is their signature and it outlasted them.

entries.name: Sassanids
entries.settlement: Ctesiphon the seat of empire; great canal-fed estates; Zoroastrian fire temples and tolerated Christians and Jews
monuments: Taq Kasra (Arch of Ctesiphon, begun under Khosrow I c. 540 CE)
trade: Roman trade in spite of wars (502-628 two centuries of conflict)
entries.beliefs: Zoroastrianism as state church; Christianity strong in the east (Church of the East); Judaism entrenched
entries.fell_by: Arab Muslim conquest: al-Qadisiyyah 636; Ctesiphon falls 637; last emperor Yazdegerd III assassinated 651
entries.notes: The Arch of Ctesiphon is the largest single-span brick vault in the premodern world; it still stands, riddled but standing.

entries.name: Abbasids
entries.settlement: round city of Baghdad founded 762; later Samarra (836-892) as purpose-built capital
monuments: Great Mosque of Samarra and the Malwiya minaret
trade: Baghdad as the largest city between Rome and China
entries.beliefs: Sunni Islam with Mutazilite and then Ashari theology; caliph as protector of the law; dhimmi compact for Christians and Jews
entries.fell_by: Mongol sack of Baghdad 1258; the caliphate survives as a title in Cairo and then Istanbul until 1924
entries.notes: Baghdad at its height held maybe a million people; the House of Wisdom. The Malwiya minaret (848) is a snail you can climb.

entries.name: Iraqi Arabs
entries.settlement: cities (Baghdad, Basra, Mosul) and date-palm villages; tribal structure persists in the countryside
trade: historically the entrepôt of the Gulf
entries.beliefs: majority Shia in the south and centre, Sunni Arab minority in the west and centre; Sufism, shrine cults
entries.notes: The dominant group of modern Iraq (~75%). The 2003 war and ISIS's 2014-2017 caliphate reshaped demographics; learn the sectarian map.

entries.name: Iraqi Kurds
entries.settlement: mountain cities (Erbil, Sulaymaniyah, Dohuk); disputed Kirkuk; autonomy since 1991, entrenched 2003-
trade: border trade with Turkey and Iran
entries.beliefs: Sunni Islam (Shafi'i) majority; Yazidi and Kakai minorities; strong Sufi orders; secular nationalism
entries.notes: Halabja 1988 (chemical attack, ~5,000 killed) is the modern Kurdish wound; Erbil Citadel is a continuously lived mound older than most cities on Earth.

entries.name: Marsh Arabs (Ma'dan)
entries.settlement: floating and stilted reed villages on artificial islands in the Tigris-Euphrates marshes
entries.beliefs: Shia Islam with deep pre-Islamic folk layers; Saint traditions
entries.notes: The drained marshes of the 1990s (~90% drained by Saddam) are partly re-flooded; Wilfred Thesiger's The Marsh Arabs (1964) is the classic portrait.

entries.name: Modern Assyrians (Syriacs)
entries.settlement: northern Iraq (Nineveh plain, Mosul, Erbil), Syria (Khabur valley), Turkey (Tur Abdin); heavy diaspora
entries.beliefs: Church of the East, Chaldean Catholic, Syriac Orthodox, Syriac Catholic — four rites of Syriac Christianity
entries.notes: They claim direct descent from Assyria. The Simele massacre (1933) and the ISIS genocide (2014, Nineveh plain) bracket a century of flight.

entries.name: Mandeans (Sabeans)
entries.settlement: riverine villages and Baghdad/Basra quarters; the smallest surviving religious community of Iraq
monuments: manda (masbuta, riverside baptismal house — often just a fenced riverbank)
crafts: gold and silver smithing (canonically their trade)
Mandaic script (a late form of cursive Aramaic)
entries.beliefs: Mandean Gnosticism: John the Baptist as the true prophet; baptism (masbuta) every Sunday; rejects Moses, Jesus and Muhammad; light emanates from Hayyi Rabbi
entries.notes: The only surviving Gnostic religion of antiquity, still practising full-immersion baptism in living rivers. Population perhaps 60-70k worldwide.

entries.name: Yazidis
entries.settlement: Sinjar mountains (Shingal) and Lalish valley; mixed villages across the Nineveh plain
monuments: Lalish temple (the holiest site, in a hidden valley)
trade: local trade; mass displacement after 2014 reduced it
entries.beliefs: Kurdish-speaking syncretic monotheism; Peacock Angel (Tawusi Melek); considered 'devil-worshippers' by hostile neighbours — a misreading of their refusal to bow to any being but God
entries.notes: ISIS's 2014 genocide of the Yazidis of Sinjar (~5,000 murdered, thousands enslaved) is the reason the world finally names them. Their temple at Lalish forbids shoes; the threshold is kissed.

entries.name: Sabians of Harran
entries.settlement: the ancient city of Harran (now in southern Turkey) and pockets elsewhere (Baghdad)
monuments: Temple of the Moon at Harran (long gone; described by medieval sources)
crafts: astronomy and mathematics (Thabit ibn Qurra; al-Battani)
entries.beliefs: star and planet worship re-read through Neoplatonism; the seven planets and zodiac; claimed the label 'Sabian' from the Quran to survive as dhimmi
entries.fell_by: pressure and conversion; community fades by the 12th-13th centuries; last individuals recorded around the Mongol era
entries.notes: Not the Mandeans, though both claimed the Quranic name 'Sabian'. Harran produced some of the greatest astronomers of the Islamic golden age.
